sections.title: Sample
sections.question: Which CEO departures are studied, how many have usable stock returns, and what were the firms like before?
sections.interpretation: The sample holds 1,501 departures with returns: 532 forced exits and 969 voluntary retirements. Firms that fire their CEO are smaller and less profitable the year before: median ROA 7.7% against 12.3% (p <0.001).

methodology.data: Gentry et al. (2021) CEO dismissal database v10Oct2024 linked to daily prices and as-reported annual statements by SEC CIK
methodology.caveat: Founder status and reasons are coded from filings, press releases and news, then checked against the sources.

sections.question: How reliable are the founder and reason codes?

sections.title: Announcement returns
sections.question: How does the stock react when the board fires the CEO, and does it matter who and why?
sections.interpretation: Over trading days -1 to +1, forced exits earn -2.3% (t = -5.26, N = 529) and retirements -0.3%. Fired founders earn -3.6% against -2.2% (gap p 0.485). Firings over a personal scandal earn -2.5%, other firings -2.3% (gap p 0.855). Prices fall -5.5% over days -30 to -2 and are flat over days +2 to +60 (-1.4%).

methodology.test: Cross-sectional t, Boehmer-Musumeci-Poulsen standardized t, Wilcoxon signed-rank; Welch t and Mann-Whitney U for differences
methodology.data: Daily total returns; market model estimated over trading days -250 to -30 for days -1 to +1; market-adjusted returns for longer windows
methodology.caveat: Day 0 is the first trading day on or after the announcement that the CEO is leaving. Firings for fraud or crime are not in the sample. Reasons other than the checked conduct labels are model codes.

tables.title: Table 5. At the announcement, a fraud dismissal is followed by a larger fall than a scandal dismissal
rows: Fired for fraud or other legal violation (comparison)
Panel B. Differences in the mean, percentage points
Personal scandal minus other firings (above zero: smaller fall after a scandal)
Personal scandal minus fraud (above zero: smaller fall after a scandal)
Panel C. Who counts as fired, and which dates
Fired, the evidence-based coding is unclear
Fired, the evidence-based coding reads not forced
Well-dated firings reweighted to resemble every firing
Every firing, any date (many days 0 misplaced)
Well-dated firings, fraud and legal violation included
tables.notes: Market-model abnormal return over trading days -1 to +1 around the announcement (day 0), on well-dated firings (dated by the database or from a dated source), fraud and legal violations excluded unless stated. N counts each row's firings. t: the t of the mean, or the Welch t of a difference; p is two-sided. Panel B: the first group's mean minus the second's; a positive number means a smaller fall in the first group. Founder, scandal and fraud labels were checked against the sources. The sex or relationship row (n = 16) is small and its test has little power. Panel C reweights by size, prior return, profitability, leverage, founder and scandal flags and year (Table IA.13).

tables.title: Table 3. Founder firms against normal firms: most of the loss comes before the announcement
rows: Panel A. Return minus the benchmark's, mean (p)
Panel B. Return minus the benchmark's, median (p)
Panel C. Dollar change against the benchmark, median per firm ($ million)
tables.notes: Founder dismissals for any reason but fraud. Each cell is the founder firm's return minus the benchmark's over the window; Section 4.1 defines the benchmarks. Days -1 to +1 use well-dated dismissals; months run from day +2. The dollar change is the return gap times the firm's market value at day -31, in 2023 dollars. In parentheses, p: one-sample t (mean) or Wilcoxon signed-rank (median), unadjusted; Table IA.5 gives intervals, the Holm adjustment and N for every window. N differs by benchmark because each needs its own data. Long-run means rest on a few firms.

tables.title: Table 4. $100 in a founder firm against $100 in normal firms, from six weeks before the dismissal
rows: Panel A. Value of $100 put in at day −31, median: founder's firm / benchmark
Panel B. Value of $100 put in at day −31, mean: founder's firm / benchmark
tables.notes: Founder dismissals for any reason but fraud. $100 is put in the founder's firm and in the benchmark at the close of trading day -31. It is valued at the close of day +1, then 12, 36 and 60 months after day +2, dividends reinvested. Each cell gives the founder's firm, then the benchmark, on the firings that have both, so the firm's value differs across rows. A delisted stock gets the delisting return of Section 4. The industry average and the three closest competitors are equal-weighted. The benchmarks are those of Table 3. N falls with the horizon as recent firings have not reached it. Medians of each column are not the median of each pair.

Each N counts the dismissals behind the number to its left. A dash marks a cell with fewer than 10 dismissals, which gets no mean or share. Panels B and C are means; Panels D and E are shares of the firms followed for 60 months.

tables.title: Table IA.4. The competitor before the firing: prior return, size and profitability
columns: Gap to competitor, points: mean; median
Value, USD bn / ROA: firm; competitor
tables.notes: The competitors of Table 3. Prior return: the mean buy-and-hold return over trading days -282 to -31; the gap is the firm's minus the competitor's, mean and median, with a paired t test (p). For the three closest competitors each measure is first averaged over the three. Value and return on assets (ROA, EBITDA over assets) are medians at the fiscal year-end before. N counts firms with a competitor. The match runs from the 4-digit SIC code to the 3-digit code to the Sharadar industry (Section 4.1).

tables.notes: The mean return gap of Table 3 with its 95% interval and one-sample t p. Holm adjusts across the five benchmarks of each window and was added after review. The winsorised mean clips returns at 1% and 99%. The benchmarks are defined in Section 4.1. Days -1 to +1 use well-dated dismissals.

tables.title: Table IA.6. Every group against its competitor: returns and dollars
columns: Against the S&P 500: return gap, mean; $ million, median
rows: Fired over performance or another reason
tables.notes: The measures of Table 3 for every group: the firm's return minus its competitor's, and that gap times the firm's market value at day -31 in 2023 dollars. Fraud firings are outside the main sample. Means and totals at 36 and 60 months rest on a few very large firms.

sections.title: Long-run returns
sections.question: Does the firm do better or worse in the 12, 36 and 60 months after the firing?
sections.interpretation: Against the market, the median forced-exit firm returns -6.0% over 12 months, -15.3% over 36 and -31.6% over 60. Against a matched firm the medians are -5.2%, -0.1% and -4.8%.

methodology.test: Wilcoxon signed-rank; skewness-adjusted t with bootstrap CI (Lyon, Barber and Tsai 1999)
methodology.data: Buy-and-hold returns from day +2, delisting returns per Shumway (1997), matched control per Barber and Lyon (1996)
methodology.caveat: Market-adjusted BHARs are skewed and negative for the typical stock; matched-firm BHARs are the main test.

tables.title: Table IA.20. Long-run returns at 12, 36 and 60 months
rows: Panel A. Median return minus the market
Panel B. Median return minus a matched firm
tables.notes: Medians of buy-and-hold returns from day +2 over 12, 36 and 60 months, all firings, with the Wilcoxon p. Panel A subtracts the market's buy-and-hold return; Panel B subtracts a matched firm in the same industry, with market value within 30 percent and the nearest return on assets. The last row gives means with t-test p; skewed returns can give means and medians of opposite sign. Delisted firms take their delisting return and then hold the market. N, 36m counts events at 36 months.

tables.title: Table IA.19. Calendar-time alpha after the announcement
rows: Fired over a personal scandal, 36 months
tables.notes: Each calendar month the portfolio holds every firm whose announcement fell 1 to H months before. Its return minus the risk-free rate is regressed on the Fama-French five factors and momentum; alpha is the intercept, with Newey-West t (6 lags). Value weights are market values at the fiscal year-end before the event. Months with fewer than 10 firms are dropped. The difference rows regress the firing portfolio's return minus the retirement portfolio's. Delisted firms take their delisting return in their last month.

tables.title: Table 7. Dismissing firms are delisted and go bankrupt far more often than retirement firms
rows: Fired for fraud or other legal violation (comparison)
Panel B. Differences in the 60-month share, percentage points
Firings minus retirements, size and profitability
tables.notes: Firms whose stock left the price file within 12, 36 and 60 months of the announcement, among firms followed that long. Taken over and Bankrupt classify the corporate action within 60 days of the final price. p vs retired: chi-square test of the 60-month share. Panel B: the 60-month gap, raw or as a linear probability coefficient with year and industry effects; N counts firings and retirements. Size and profitability: log market value and return on assets. Every control adds the prior return, leverage, book-to-market, distress and loss. Table IA.18 adds the checks.

tables.title: Table 6. Dismissing firms are delisted more often than retirement firms in every size band
rows: All, bankruptcies within 180 days of the announcement set aside
tables.notes: Market value at the fiscal year-end before the departure, in US dollars. Delisted: the stock left the price file (taken over, bankrupt or other) within 60 months of the announcement. Bankrupt: the corporate action within 60 days of the final price was a bankruptcy or liquidation. p is a chi-square test of the share gone, firings against retirements. The last row sets aside firms whose bankruptcy was recorded within 180 days after the announcement, which were already failing when the CEO left. Only events with a complete 60-month horizon enter.

sections.title: The board afterwards
sections.question: What happens to the board about two years after the firing?
sections.interpretation: About two years after a forced exit, 48.0% of the earlier directors are gone, against 37.8% after a retirement (p <0.001).

sections.title: Robustness
sections.question: Do the results survive other models, samples and definitions?
sections.interpretation: With five factors plus momentum the founder gap is -1.4 percentage points (p 0.516) and the personal-scandal gap 0.6 percentage points (p 0.564). On the 196 exits the evidence also reads as forced, the return is -1.7%.

tables.notes: Firing effect with controls: the coefficient on the firing dummy in a linear probability model with log market value, return on assets (ROA) in fiscal year -1, event-year and Fama-French industry effects, standard errors clustered by year. The matched row compares each firing firm with its own matched firm (paired t). The rows marked same controls add the prior 12-month return, leverage, book-to-market, an Altman Z distress flag and a loss flag, on the firms with every item; the founder and personal-scandal rows estimate that model within firings. Evidence agreeing or unclear: firings as the evidence-based coding reads them, against retirements. Hazard ratios: Cox model, every month of follow-up to 60 months, industry strata; above one, firing firms leave sooner.

sections.title: Growth after the dismissal
sections.question: Does the firm grow more slowly than its competitor after a founder or scandal dismissal?
sections.interpretation: Against the matched competitor, the median founder firm's revenue growth changes by -0.6 percentage points a year to year +3 (p 0.670, N = 30) and the median hired-CEO firm's by 0.0 percentage points (N = 636); the difference in medians has p 0.634. After a personal scandal the median change is 0.8 percentage points (N = 25).

methodology.test: Wilcoxon signed-rank, one-sample t, Welch t, Mann-Whitney U, Holm across 14 tests; OLS with controls, clustered by firm
methodology.data: Sharadar SF1 as-reported annual statements, fiscal years -3 to +5 around the dismissal year
methodology.caveat: Difference-in-differences against the closest competitor. Ratios use firms still filing; revenue, asset and market value growth are also reported with bankrupt firms and regulatory delistings at -100%. Employees are not in the data.
